The best answer for chronic back pain is actually a series of stretching and other mobility exercises. It hurts - but it is going to continue to hurt until you get everything back properly realigned, and then give the body a chance to heal with everything in the proper place.

The body can and will heal back injury - and can compensate for almost anything short of severe spinal cord damage. (We are learning how to repair even that these days.)

One of the things that happens, that is very common, is you injure a site, and then continue to re-injure it, for years - such that the area always remains inflamed, and the pain remains fairly constant. Pain is almost always pressure on a nerve - but the point were you feel the pain is not always the location of the actual injury. The inflammation is actually your body trying to push the bones back into place - and the meds serve only to mask the pain or to reduce the immune system reaction - which hinders it's work.

The thing is, if you get the bones back into place - then the swelling goes down, and the pain is gone. The area is still weak, so it is easy to re-injure it again. You not only have to get everything back into place, you have to continue the strengthening exercises long after the pain is gone.

So, I have seen the best success with a combination of first chiropractic assessment - they can often spot the actual problem areas - and then physio therapy - experts at getting things strong and moving again. Also - if you've got some arthritic factors going on then you also need to look at diet and dietary supplements - because you may have some food related allergic reaction as well - triggering immune system response.

There are also neural pathway considerations in long term chronic pain - because the brain forms powerful pathways due to constant use. Those pathways get cross wired with other pathways used in your life such that the pain pathway can be triggered by using the other pathways. A strong neural pathway will atrophy and die off when you cease to use it, as it should - but stronger pathways take a lot more time to stop signalling - from several months to years. Even so, the pain levels experienced once the injury itself is actually healed will diminish as time passes. If this happens in your case - first get the injury healed - then you have to spot for and identify triggers that are triggering that pathway - this is actually a very good time for excessive meds (after the injury is repaired) - because the less the neural pathway is signalling, the sooner it will die off.

Even severe repetitive strain injury can be fully repaired in such a manner.

Post Script - it is important to realize that the bones themselves are alive - they are a living dynamic system - not unlike concrete that repairs itself - the same is true for cartilage, skin, etc. The body has a map written in the DNA, and it tries to keep to that map - and it will add and subtract any kind of tissue (bone is like supper slow motion tissue) in order to meet the map design. If we could get the body to do this with teeth that would be a huge breakthrough. Much of this repair work occurs while you are sleeping - so get as much sleep as you can.
